doc.title: Oscar Peterson interviewed by Joe Williams, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

title: Recording West Side Story, twice, for Verve
summary: While teaching in Toronto the trio arranged and recorded the album in New York, then Peterson insisted on redoing it the next day.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Yes he did, he wrote an album for me.

An album, yeah, yeah. And I must say, your “West Side Story” touches, I mean it’s poignant when it needs to be poignant, it says so much, feeling and glory and happiness, and all the facets. You show it at the piano, and with your group, and with the people you work with.
Well I have to tell you the story on “West Side Story,” on that album. We had this school, the jazz school in Toronto, called The Advanced School for Contemporary Music, and it

was Ray Brown, Ed Thigpen and myself. And we were teaching there. And I got a call from Verve records and they said, “we would like you to do something on ‘West Side Story.’” And I said, oh, boy, I’d heard some of the score and that’s not easy, you know. So they said, “could you put something together and we’d like to do it soon, because the show is hot, and we’d like to get it out.” You know like record companies, it’s like do it yesterday. So while we were teaching, on off periods, I would call the group together in the school and we’d get in a room somewhere, and we’d put together arrangements on the album. We flew into New York, we arranged that we’d fly in I think it was on a Tuesday, and we said, okay there are no classes, just study periods all day Tuesday we’ll be away, we’ll be back Wednesday. We flew into New York and we started the session in the early afternoon, and we finished the album. We finished the album. And they didn’t play back tune for tune for tune, we just came back in and listened to it. I just sat and listened to it and they ran through the album, and I said, I remember saying to Jim Davis, I said, “can we have the studio tomorrow?” He said, “I don’t know, we’ll get it for you if you need it,” he says, “why?” I said, “I want to do the album over.” He said, “well you finished the album.” I said, “not really.” It didn’t sit right, you know, it just did not sit right. So we got together the next day and we cut the album that you are referring to, and you could obviously hear the difference between the two performances. You know there was just something not there on the first one that was there on the second. And I’m glad I did it over.
Oh, yes. Tenderness, fire, and beauty. I know that the composer, Bernstein, I know he loved it. I know he loved it you know. To hear his music interpreted like that.
We were almost supposed to do something with him with that. I wish we had had the chance.
